title: CompletableFuture & Async (T2)
scopeHtml: Composition operators, which thread runs which stage, exception handling, timeouts and cancellation limits, blocking in async stages, context propagation, and a brief comparison with reactive and virtual threads (deep dive in the Virtual Threads chunk).

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between thenApply and thenCompose on a CompletableFuture? When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the map vs flatMap test. Candidates who mix them up produce CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>> or accidentally serialize work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "thenApply takes a function from a value to a plain value, like map. thenCompose takes a function from a value to another CompletionStage, like flatMap, and flattens it so I get one future instead of a nested one. If my next step is itself asynchronous, I use thenCompose; if it is a cheap in-memory transformation, thenApply."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A CompletableFuture<T> is a box that will eventually hold a value or an exception. Each thenXxx method registers a dependent stage that fires when the source completes and returns a new future for that stage.

Method Function shape Result type
thenApply(Function<T,U>) T -> U CF<U>
thenCompose(Function<T,CompletionStage<U>>) T -> CF<U> CF<U> (flattened)
thenAccept(Consumer<T>) T -> void CF<Void>
thenRun(Runnable) () -> void CF<Void>
thenCombine(other, BiFunction) (T,U) -> V CF<V>

With thenApply(id -> loadOrderAsync(id)) the function returns a future, so the result is CF<CF<Order>>. The outer future completes as soon as the inner future object is created, not when the order is loaded. Anyone who does .join() on the outer gets back an unfinished inner future. thenCompose subscribes to the returned stage and completes the outer future only when the inner one completes, and it also propagates the inner exception.

thenCompose is also the dependency operator: step B needs step A's output, so B cannot start until A is done. Latency is the sum. If steps are independent, do not chain them with thenCompose; start both and join them with thenCombine (see the fan-out question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: nested future, and the join returns before the order is loaded
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>> bad =
    userIdFuture.thenApply(id -> loadOrderAsync(id));

// Correct: flattened
CompletableFuture<Order> order =
    userIdFuture.thenCompose(id -> loadOrderAsync(id));

// Correct use of thenApply: cheap pure transform
CompletableFuture<String> label = order.thenApply(o -> o.id() + ":" + o.status());

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using thenApply and then calling .join() inside the lambda to "unwrap" the inner future. This blocks a pool thread (see the blocking-in-stage question).
  • Chaining independent calls with thenCompose, turning a parallel fan-out into a sequential one.
  • Doing heavy or blocking work in thenApply and assuming it is "async". It is not; it runs on whichever thread completes the source (or the caller).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does thenCompose do if the function throws? → The returned future completes exceptionally with a CompletionException wrapping it, same as thenApply.
  2. What is thenCompose's relationship to flatMap? → Same monadic bind; thenApply is map, and thenCompose is flatMap over the future.
  3. How do you recover with another async call after a failure? → exceptionallyCompose (Java 12+), the async counterpart of exceptionally; on Java 8-11 use handle(...).thenCompose(Function.identity()).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "compose is like flatMap". The senior adds that compose expresses a data dependency and therefore sequential latency, that independent calls belong in thenCombine/allOf, and that neither operator moves the work to another thread by itself.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service that built an order summary with five chained thenCompose calls on independent downstream lookups had p99 equal to the sum of five calls. Switching to parallel start plus thenCombine cut it to the max of the five.

questions.promptHtml: If I call CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> callService()) with no executor, where does it run, and why is that a problem in a backend service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most CompletableFuture production incidents are shared-pool incidents. This checks whether you know the default and its sizing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), a JVM-wide shared pool whose parallelism is roughly cores minus one. It is sized for CPU-bound work, so if I put blocking IO on it, a few slow calls can starve everything else on the JVM that uses the common pool, including parallel streams. For IO I pass my own bounded executor."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Java 21 Javadoc says that async methods without an explicit Executor use ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), unless the common pool does not support a parallelism of at least two, in which case a new Thread is created per task. Subclasses can change this by overriding defaultExecutor().

Common pool parallelism defaults to availableProcessors() - 1 (verify for your exact JDK; it can be overridden with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N). So a 4-core container gets 3 workers. The pool threads are daemon threads. The pool can compensate for blocked workers only when blocking is signalled through ForkJoinPool.managedBlock; plain Thread.sleep, JDBC or HTTP calls do not signal it.

What else uses the same pool: parallel streams, CompletableFuture default async, Arrays.parallelSort, and any library that uses the common pool. One misbehaving feature starves the rest.

 4 cores -> commonPool parallelism = 3
 3 requests each blocking 2s on HTTP inside supplyAsync
 -> all 3 workers busy 2s; request #4's stage waits in the queue
 -> parallel streams elsewhere in the JVM also stall

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ExecutorService io = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    32, 32, 0L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
    new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("io-%d").build(), // Guava
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());

CompletableFuture<Resp> f = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.call(), io);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming supplyAsync has its own pool per application. It is JVM-wide.
  • Passing the executor to the first stage only; later thenApplyAsync calls without an executor jump back to the common pool.
  • Unbounded Executors.newCachedThreadPool() as the "fix", which converts starvation into a thread explosion.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you see the problem? → Thread dump shows ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-N threads parked in socket reads; ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getQueuedSubmissionCount() grows.
  2. On a 1-vCPU container, what happens? → Parallelism is below two, so the Javadoc behavior applies: a new thread per async task, with no pooling or bound.
  3. Can you make the default executor yours globally? → Not for static supplyAsync; wrap with your own factory or subclass and override defaultExecutor().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it uses the ForkJoinPool". The senior knows it is shared and CPU-sized, knows the 1-CPU container edge case, and always injects named, bounded executors per dependency (bulkhead).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's search endpoint used supplyAsync for HTTP calls; a slow downstream parked all three common-pool workers and an unrelated parallel-stream report job in the same JVM timed out.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between thenApply and thenApplyAsync? Which thread runs each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Which thread am I on?" is the root of most CompletableFuture bugs (blocking a Netty thread, losing thread-locals).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "thenApply runs the function on whichever thread completes the source future, or on the caller's thread if the source is already complete when I attach the stage. thenApplyAsync always submits the function to an executor, the common pool by default or one I pass. So plain thenApply gives no guarantee about the thread; Async gives a hop to a pool."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each stage is stored as a completion object in the source's stack. When the source completes, the completing thread pops and runs dependents inline (that is the non-async path). If the source was already done when thenApply is called, the function runs immediately in the calling thread.

Case Thread that runs fn
thenApply, source not yet complete The thread that calls complete/finishes the source
thenApply, source already complete The thread calling thenApply
thenApplyAsync(fn) commonPool (or defaultExecutor())
thenApplyAsync(fn, ex) ex

Consequence: if the completing thread is an HTTP client IO thread (Netty event loop, Apache async client reactor), a heavy or blocking thenApply runs on that IO thread and blocks the client. The usual rule is: do cheap non-blocking work in non-async stages; do anything heavy with an Async variant and an explicit executor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CompletableFuture<String> cf = new CompletableFuture<>();
cf.thenApply(s -> { log(Thread.currentThread().getName()); return s; });
new Thread(() -> cf.complete("x"), "completer").start(); // logs "completer"

CompletableFuture<String> done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("y");
done.thenApply(s -> { log(Thread.currentThread().getName()); return s; }); // caller thread

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming thenApply after supplyAsync runs "in the background" on the pool every time. If the pool thread has not yet finished it does; if it already finished it runs on the caller.
  • Sprinkling Async everywhere "to be safe". Each hop costs a queue handoff and loses thread-locals.
  • Forgetting the executor argument on the Async variant.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the same code log different thread names across runs? → Race between completion and attach: whichever happens last runs the stage.
  2. Does thenApplyAsync guarantee order for several dependents of one future? → No; dependents of the same source are not run in a guaranteed order.
  3. How can inline stage execution cause deep stack traces? → Long chains completed by one thread run recursively; the implementation unrolls much of it, but a stage that completes another future inline can still nest, so keep stages short.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Async runs in another thread". Senior: gives the three-case thread table, ties it to blocking IO event loops and thread-local loss, and chooses non-async vs async per stage deliberately.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A thenApply doing a JSON deserialization of a 5 MB body ran on the HTTP client's IO thread and stalled all connections on that thread, showing up as random 200 ms latency spikes.

questions.subtopic: Manual completion and Future vs CompletableFuture
questions.promptHtml: How is CompletableFuture different from the plain Future, and how do you complete one manually (for example from a callback-based client)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can adapt callback APIs and know why Future.get() is not composable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Future can only be polled or blocked on with get(). CompletableFuture supports non-blocking callbacks, composition and manual completion. I can create an empty one with new CompletableFuture<>() and call complete(value) or completeExceptionally(t) from a callback to bridge any callback API into the future world."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CompletableFuture<T> implements both Future<T> and CompletionStage<T>. Key points:

  • complete(v) returns true only for the first caller; later calls are no-ops. Same for completeExceptionally. This makes it safe for racing completions (first-wins), e.g. primary vs hedged request.
  • cancel(boolean) is just completeExceptionally(new CancellationException()); the boolean has no effect.
  • get() throws checked ExecutionException; join() throws unchecked CompletionException. Both wrap the real cause.
  • failedFuture(ex) (Java 9) and completedFuture(v) are for returning pre-completed values from methods.
  • copy() gives a new future that cannot be completed by callers if you hand it out, and minimalCompletionStage() hides the mutating methods entirely.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CompletableFuture<Response> toFuture(AsyncHttpClient client, Request req) {
    CompletableFuture<Response> cf = new CompletableFuture<>();
    client.execute(req, new Callback() {
        public void onSuccess(Response r) { cf.complete(r); }
        public void onFailure(Throwable t) { cf.completeExceptionally(t); }
    });
    return cf;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not completing the future on every path (for example a missing catch in the callback), leaving callers waiting forever. Add a timeout.
  • Returning your internal CompletableFuture to callers who can then call complete() on it. Return copy() or a CompletionStage.
  • Expecting cancel(true) to interrupt the running task.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does get() do with the exception? → Throws ExecutionException with the original as cause; join() throws CompletionException.
  2. How would you implement first-wins across two replicas? → Two futures plus anyOf, or both call target.complete(...); first wins, then ignore/cancel the loser.
  3. Why might a never-completed future leak? → Dependents hold references to lambdas and captured state in the future's stack; without completion they are retained as long as the future is reachable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists get() vs callbacks. Senior covers first-writer-wins completion semantics, API hygiene (copy, CompletionStage in signatures) and the never-completed leak.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A callback bridge missed the onTimeout path; the future never completed, request threads waited on get() with no timeout and the pool drained over an hour.

questions.promptHtml: How do you run several independent calls in parallel and combine the results with CompletableFuture? What are the gotchas of allOf and anyOf?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Fan-out aggregation is the most common real use case, and allOf/anyOf have surprising signatures.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I start all the calls first, then combine them. For two I use thenCombine. For N, allOf returns CompletableFuture<Void>, so I collect each future's result with join() after allOf completes. anyOf returns CompletableFuture<Object> and completes with the first to finish, which can be an exception, not necessarily a success. Neither cancels the other futures."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Start before combine. Futures are hot: supplyAsync starts immediately. Parallelism comes from creating all futures before waiting on any.
  • allOf(f1..fn) completes when all complete. If any completes exceptionally, the returned future completes exceptionally (with a CompletionException whose cause is one of the failures), but only after all have finished. So it is not fail-fast.
  • anyOf completes with the first to complete, normally or exceptionally. Its type is Object, so you cast. If the first to finish is a fast failure, you get the failure even if another would have succeeded soon.
  • Neither operator cancels slower futures; they keep running and consuming pool threads.

Latency math: three independent calls of 80, 120, 200 ms sequential via thenCompose is 400 ms; parallel with allOf is about 200 ms (max, plus scheduling).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CompletableFuture<User> u = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> users.get(id), io);
CompletableFuture<List<Order>> o = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orders.get(id), io);
CompletableFuture<Prefs> p = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prefs.get(id), io);

CompletableFuture<Profile> profile = CompletableFuture.allOf(u, o, p)
    .thenApply(v -> new Profile(u.join(), o.join(), p.join())); // join is safe: all done

// Two futures
CompletableFuture<Integer> total = a.thenCombine(b, Integer::sum);

// First successful: anyOf does NOT do this
CompletableFuture<Object> first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(r1, r2);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing list.stream().map(CompletableFuture::supplyAsync...).map(CompletableFuture::join) in one stream, which serializes (see the spot-the-bug scenario).
  • Assuming allOf fails fast. It waits for every future, including slow ones.
  • Using anyOf as "first success" without filtering failures.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get "first success"? → Wrap each with exceptionally/handle into a custom future and complete a shared future only on success, completing exceptionally only when all failed.
  2. How do you get partial results when some fail? → handle or exceptionally per future into Optional/default before allOf.
  3. How do you fail fast on the first failure? → Complete a shared future from each future's whenComplete, cancelling the others yourself.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average shows allOf plus join. Senior states it is not fail-fast, anyOf returns exceptions as first result, and futures keep running afterward, so adds per-call timeouts and per-future fallbacks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An aggregator used anyOf across two cache replicas; a replica returning an immediate error "won" every time and users saw errors although the other replica was healthy.

questions.promptHtml: Explain exceptionally, handle and whenComplete. What does CompletionException wrapping do to your exception handling?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: People write catch (MyException e) around join() and wonder why it never matches, or swallow errors in chains.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "exceptionally runs only on failure and replaces the result with a fallback. handle runs always with (value, exception) and returns a new value. whenComplete runs always but cannot change the result; it is for side effects like logging, and the original outcome flows through. In dependent stages the exception is wrapped in a CompletionException, so I unwrap with getCause() before checking the type."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Method Runs when Can change outcome Typical use
exceptionally(fn) failure only yes, to a value fallback
handle((v,ex) -> r) always yes (value or recover) map both paths
whenComplete((v,ex) -> {}) always no (but see below) logging, metrics, cleanup
exceptionallyCompose (12+) failure only yes, to a new async stage async fallback

Wrapping rules: if a stage's function throws, the stage completes with a CompletionException wrapping it. When that propagates to downstream stages, they receive the CompletionException. A future completed with completeExceptionally(ex) hands the raw ex to handlers attached directly to it, but dependents see it wrapped. supplyAsync wraps the thrown exception in a CompletionException even for handlers attached directly (verify on your JDK with a quick test). join() throws CompletionException; get() throws ExecutionException; both carry the cause. Cancellation surfaces as CancellationException.

whenComplete subtlety: if the source succeeded but the action throws, the returned future fails with that exception. If the source failed, the original exception is kept and the action's exception is only attached as suppressed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Throwable unwrap(Throwable t) {
    while ((t instanceof CompletionException || t instanceof ExecutionException)
           && t.getCause() != null) t = t.getCause();
    return t;
}

fetch()
  .whenComplete((v, ex) -> metrics.record(ex == null))        // side effect only
  .exceptionally(ex -> unwrap(ex) instanceof TimeoutException ? CACHED : rethrow(ex));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• exceptionally(ex -> ex instanceof MyEx ? ... ) never matches because ex is a CompletionException.
  • Placing exceptionally early in the chain, which swallows the error and lets later stages run with the fallback silently.
  • Expecting whenComplete to recover from errors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you rethrow from exceptionally? → Throw an unchecked exception or return failedFuture through exceptionallyCompose; it re-wraps.
  2. What does handle receive for cancellation? → A CancellationException (possibly wrapped downstream).
  3. How do you ensure a fire-and-forget chain does not drop errors? → End with whenComplete that logs, or a terminal exceptionally that logs and reports metrics; nothing else observes an unattached failure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists the three methods. Senior covers wrapping semantics, the first-vs-downstream difference, whenComplete throwing, and the "silent failure in unobserved chain" risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payment confirmation pipeline ended in thenAccept(sendEmail) with no terminal handler; a template exception was never logged and thousands of confirmations were silently skipped.

questions.contextHtml:
A product-page endpoint fetches prices for up to 20 SKUs from a pricing service (each call about 100 ms). The team "parallelized" it with CompletableFuture. At 200 RPS, the endpoint p50 is 2.1 s for 20 SKUs, and the pricing service shows concurrency of 1 per request. The code:

List<Price> prices = skus.stream()
    .map(sku -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(sku), io))
    .map(CompletableFuture::join)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

The io pool has 32 threads. CPU is 15%. The load balancer shows no errors.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it slow, and how do you fix it? What else would you check before shipping?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The pool is too small, increase it." Wrong: 32 threads were barely used. It also misses that the stream pipeline processes element by element.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 2.1 s about 20 x 100 ms? (That matches 2.0 s, so it points to serialization.) Does pricing accept batch calls? What is pricing's rate limit? What should happen on partial failure?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage, so ship the fix quickly. If urgent, cap SKUs per page.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Stream laziness serializes the stages; (b) pool too small; (c) pricing slow under load; (d) connection pool exhausted. The numbers favor (a): 20 x 100 ms = 2.0 s, observed 2.1 s, CPU low, downstream concurrency 1.
  4. How I'd verify each: Thread dump shows only one io- thread busy per request; log timestamps of call starts, which are 100 ms apart. Check pricing's per-request concurrency in its metrics.
  5. Root cause: Streams process each element through the whole pipeline before pulling the next one for sequential streams. For element 1, supplyAsync is submitted and then join() blocks before element 2 is even mapped. So at most one call is in flight.
  6. Fix: Materialize all futures first, then join.
List<CompletableFuture<Price>> fs = skus.stream()
    .map(sku -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(sku), io))
    .toList();                                   // terminal op: all started
List<Price> prices = fs.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();

Expected latency about 100 ms plus queueing. Long-term: use a batch endpoint (one call for 20 SKUs), per-call orTimeout, and bound concurrency per request so one request cannot take 20 of 32 pool threads. 7. Prevention: Code review checklist: "no join in the same stream as submission"; a unit test with a fake service sleeping 100 ms asserting total under 300 ms; a metric for fan-out width. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just enlarge the pool: 200 RPS x 20 calls = 4,000 concurrent calls in the worst case against a pricing service nobody sized for that. Parallelism multiplies downstream load (20x amplification); coordinate with pricing's owners.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One of 20 calls fails; do we fail the page? → Per-future exceptionally returning "price unavailable" and a degraded flag, if product accepts it.
  • Parallel stream instead? → It would use the common pool, which suits CPU work, and would throttle at cores-1 for IO. Avoid.
  • Pricing latency rises to 1 s? → With the 32-thread pool, 200 RPS x 20 calls x 1 s = 4,000 busy threads required (Little's law), so the pool would saturate; need batching, caching or load shedding.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A catalog service looked parallel in code review, yet traces showed a staircase pattern of spans. One join in the wrong place in a stream had defeated the whole design; a trace waterfall found it in minutes where code reading had not.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Increases thread pool, no explanation of the serialization.
  • Hire: Identifies stream laziness and fixes with collect-then-join; mentions timeouts.
  • Strong hire: Also computes the downstream amplification with Little's law, proposes batching and per-request bounding, and adds a test that would have caught it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you put a timeout on a CompletableFuture? What does orTimeout actually do to the underlying work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every remote call needs a deadline. Candidates often believe a timeout also stops the work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Since Java 9, orTimeout(t, unit) completes the future exceptionally with TimeoutException if it is not done in time, and completeOnTimeout(value, t, unit) completes it normally with a default. Both only change the future. The task already running on a pool thread keeps going, so I also need a real timeout on the underlying client call. On Java 8 there is no built-in, so I use a scheduler."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
orTimeout schedules a task on a JDK-internal single daemon scheduler thread that, at the deadline, calls completeExceptionally(new TimeoutException()) if the future is not done. If the future completes first, the timer is cancelled. Mechanism:

 t=0    supplyAsync(callRemote) -> worker thread W blocks in socket read
 t=2s   timer thread: cf.completeExceptionally(TimeoutException)
        dependents run (fallback etc.) - caller continues
 t=30s  W finally returns; result discarded (future already completed)

So at t=2 s the caller has moved on, but W is still occupied for 28 more seconds, which is exactly how timeouts without client-level timeouts still exhaust pools. A past bug, JDK-8303742, was a leak in which an exceptionally-completed orTimeout future did not cancel its timeout task; it was fixed in 21 per the OpenJDK mailing list (verify the exact backport versions if you run older JDKs).

Where to place the timeout: right after the specific call, not at the end of a long chain, so you know which dependency timed out. A deadline for the whole request is separate: compute remaining budget and pass it down (deadline propagation).

Layers of timeouts: connect timeout, read/socket timeout, request timeout on the client (stops the IO), then orTimeout as a backstop for the future.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Java 9+
CompletableFuture<Price> p = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(sku), io)        // pricing client has its own 1.5s read timeout
    .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .exceptionally(ex -> Price.UNAVAILABLE);

// completeOnTimeout: default value instead of an exception
var rec = recommender.fetchAsync(userId).completeOnTimeout(List.of(), 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Relying on orTimeout alone and leaving the HTTP client at its default (often infinite or very long) read timeout.
  • Using future.get(2, SECONDS): this throws on the caller's side but leaves the future running; and it blocks a thread.
  • Applying one orTimeout at the end and not knowing which stage was slow.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Java 8 equivalent? → A ScheduledExecutorService that calls completeExceptionally, or Resilience4j TimeLimiter.
  2. What thread runs the fallback after a timeout? → The timer's thread (the thread that completes the future) unless you use an Async variant; keep timeout callbacks cheap or hop executors.
  3. How would you cancel the downstream call? → Hold a handle (for example the client's call object) and cancel it in whenComplete when the future timed out.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "orTimeout throws after N seconds". Senior: it abandons the wait, not the work; layers client timeouts, hedges the thread-leak risk, and thinks in deadlines for the whole request.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Calls "timed out" at 2 s in the app but the HTTP client waited 60 s; in-flight work accumulated and the pool of 50 threads sat fully occupied by abandoned calls.

questions.promptHtml: Why is calling join() or get() inside a CompletableFuture stage dangerous? Show how it deadlocks a bounded pool.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Thread-pool starvation deadlock is a classic senior-level failure mode that does not need any lock.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A stage that blocks on another future occupies a pool thread while waiting. If the future it waits for needs a thread from the same bounded pool, and all threads are already waiting, nothing can run: pool-starvation deadlock. The fix is to compose with thenCompose instead of blocking, or run dependent work on a different pool."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
No lock is held, so jstack will not report a deadlock. Picture a pool with 2 threads:

 pool = [T1, T2]
 T1: stageA -> joins innerA   (innerA queued, needs a thread)
 T2: stageB -> joins innerB   (innerB queued, needs a thread)
 queue: [innerA, innerB]  -> no free thread -> both wait forever

With a bigger pool it manifests as load-dependent: at low RPS it works, at high RPS all workers are waiting on children still in the queue. The ForkJoinPool common pool can compensate for some blocking only if the waiting uses ForkJoinPool.managedBlock (CompletableFuture.join() called from a FJ worker does use managedBlock in the JDK implementation, which is why this bug is often hidden on the common pool but hits ThreadPoolExecutor; verify behaviour on your JDK before relying on it).

Even without deadlock, blocking wastes a thread for the duration of the child call, so throughput = threads / blocking-time (Little's law), and the async design brings no benefit.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

// Broken: parent stage blocks on child scheduled on same pool
CompletableFuture<String> parent = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() ->
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "child", pool).join(), pool);
// Two such parents occupy both threads; both children wait in the queue.

// Fixed: compose
CompletableFuture<String> ok = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> prepare(), pool)
    .thenCompose(x -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> child(x), pool));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Blocking in thenApply to "unwrap" a nested future.
  • Using a single-thread executor for both orchestration and IO.
  • Assuming a deadlock detector will find it; thread dumps show threads WAITING in CompletableFuture$Signaller.block.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you find it live? → Thread dump: all pool threads in CompletableFuture.waitingGet/join, executor queue length nonzero and not draining.
  2. Does a bigger pool fix it? → It only moves the failure threshold; remove the blocking.
  3. Where is blocking acceptable? → At the edge, once, on a thread that is not part of the async pool (for example the request thread calling join on the final future).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "blocking is bad". Senior produces the mechanism (children queued behind blocked parents), recognizes it as a non-lock deadlock, and designs separate pools for orchestration vs IO.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fan-out service used one 16-thread pool for both orchestration and leaf calls; under a traffic spike every thread was a parent waiting on queued leaves and the service went silent with zero CPU.

questions.promptHtml: How do you size and configure the executor you pass to CompletableFuture stages, and what happens when it is saturated?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests that you apply thread-pool fundamentals (Little's law, bounded queues, rejection) to async pipelines.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I use a dedicated bounded ThreadPoolExecutor per dependency class. For IO-bound calls, threads ≈ target throughput x average latency (Little's law), with a small bounded queue and a rejection policy I chose deliberately. When saturated, a rejected submission throws RejectedExecutionException at the supplyAsync call site, which I must turn into a failed future or fast 503, not an uncaught exception."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sizing example: target 500 calls/s to a dependency at 80 ms average latency means 500 x 0.08 = 40 concurrent calls, so about 40 threads, plus headroom (say 50) and a queue of maybe 100 (2 s of backlog at 50 calls/s of excess is too much; pick it from your latency SLO). CPU-bound stages: about cores, or cores + 1.

Behaviour on saturation depends on policy:

Policy Effect on CF
AbortPolicy (default) supplyAsync throws RejectedExecutionException synchronously from the submitting thread
CallerRunsPolicy Task runs on the submitting thread: backpressure, but it may block a request or event-loop thread
DiscardPolicy Task silently dropped: the future never completes (worst case)
Custom Return a failed future, count a metric

DiscardPolicy with CompletableFuture produces futures that never complete; avoid it. With AbortPolicy, wrap the submission:

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<T> CompletableFuture<T> submit(Supplier<T> task) {
    try {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, io);
    } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
        return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new OverloadedException("io pool full", e));
    }
}

Name threads, export pool metrics (active, queue size, rejected count) via Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n): its queue is unbounded, so overload becomes memory growth and multi-second latency, not rejection.
  • Sharing one pool across unrelated dependencies, so one slow dependency starves the others (no bulkhead).
  • CallerRunsPolicy when callers are Netty event-loop threads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why bounded queue? → To fail fast; unbounded queue hides saturation until memory or latency explodes.
  2. How do you decide queue size? → Max acceptable wait / service time x threads; typically small.
  3. Timeouts and a full queue? → Queue wait counts toward the caller's deadline; a task that waited past its deadline should be dropped at dequeue.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use a fixed thread pool of 10-20". Senior derives from Little's law, bounds the queue, picks rejection by caller type, and surfaces saturation as a metric and fast failure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An unbounded queue behind a slow dependency grew to 400k tasks; the heap filled and the service OOMed instead of shedding load at the edge.

questions.promptHtml: You log with MDC (request ID, user ID) and use Spring Security's context. After moving work to a CompletableFuture on another pool the IDs vanish from the logs. Why, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests understanding that thread-local state is bound to a thread, not to a logical request, and knowledge of real propagation mechanisms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "MDC, SecurityContextHolder and tracing context live in thread-locals. A pool thread has its own, so values set on the request thread are not there. I capture the context on the submitting thread, restore it around the task on the worker thread and clear it afterwards. I do this once in a wrapping executor, or use a library such as Micrometer's context-propagation or Spring's DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Capture happens when you submit (request thread), restore when it runs (worker thread). With CompletableFuture there are two sets of points: the initial supplyAsync and every Async stage, but also non-async stages that run on whichever thread completes the source, which may be a thread with someone else's context.

 request thread: MDC{reqId=42}
   supplyAsync(task, wrapped) ---capture {reqId=42}--->
                                   worker: set MDC; run; finally restore previous/clear

Mechanisms:

  • Wrapping executor: decorate every Runnable submitted: captured = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); run(() -> { prev = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); set(captured); try { r.run(); } finally { restore(prev) } }).
  • Spring Security: DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService / DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable.
  • Micrometer context-propagation library: ContextExecutorService/ContextSnapshot capture registered ThreadLocalAccessors (MDC, observation, security) in one go. Check the docs for the exact Spring Boot version, as the integration points differ (verify).
  • Tracing: MDC fields like trace ID are only a view; the actual span context must also be propagated (OpenTelemetry Context.taskWrapping(executor)), or child spans will be orphaned.

Dependent stages without an executor argument still run inline on the completing thread, which restores nothing; if the completing thread is a different pool thread, the context seen there is whatever that pool restored for its own task.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MdcExecutor implements Executor {
    private final Executor delegate;
    MdcExecutor(Executor d) { this.delegate = d; }
    public void execute(Runnable r) {
        Map<String,String> ctx = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();     // request thread
        delegate.execute(() -> {
            Map<String,String> prev = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
            if (ctx != null) MDC.setContextMap(ctx); else MDC.clear();
            try { r.run(); }
            finally { if (prev != null) MDC.setContextMap(prev); else MDC.clear(); }
        });
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Copying the context but never clearing it, so the next task on that pooled thread logs another user's ID (data leak across requests).
  • Wrapping only the first stage.
  • Mutating the same Map instance shared between threads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not InheritableThreadLocal? → It copies at thread creation, not task submission; pooled threads never refresh it.
  2. What about ScopedValue? → Bound for a scope and inherited by structured-concurrency subtasks; still a preview API in 21-24 (verify the status in your release), and not a drop-in for pools.
  3. How do you test propagation? → Integration test asserting a log appender's MDC in a stage and a clean MDC after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "pass the request ID as a parameter" (acceptable but invasive). Senior wraps the executor centrally, restores previous state, covers security and tracing context, and notes non-async stage hazards.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Logs for 5% of requests carried the wrong user ID because a wrapper set MDC but never cleared it; support engineers chased the wrong account for two days.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout service (6 pods, 8 vCPU each, ~400 RPS total) added a CompletableFuture step that calls a fraud API. Since release, three things are reported: (1) logs from the fraud step have no traceId, (2) audit logs show userId=u-7731 on a request belonging to another user, roughly 0.3% of requests, (3) SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() is null in the fraud step, causing 401s from an internal API that needs the caller identity. The wrapper they added:

Executor ctxExec = r -> { MDC.setContextMap(captured); pool.execute(r); }; // captured = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap() at construction

captured is a static field assigned in the first request after boot.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose all three symptoms and propose the fix and prevention plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the request ID to the method parameters" and nothing about the wrong user ID, which shows the leak is the serious part.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which executor runs the fraud stage and is the same pool used by other features? Does the wrong userId correlate with a particular pool thread name? Spring Security's strategy (default MODE_THREADLOCAL)? Is the log field from MDC or from the tracing library?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The wrong userId in audit logs is a data-integrity and privacy issue, so I'd disable the async fraud path via feature flag or revert, and flag the compliance team.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The wrapper sets MDC on the submitting thread (not the worker) and uses a static snapshot from the first request; (b) MDC never cleared on pool threads so stale values persist; (c) security context not propagated at all; (d) trace context orphaned because only MDC was handled.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the wrapper: MDC.setContextMap(captured) runs inside execute, i.e. on the caller, not in the runnable. Reproduce with a test hitting two users concurrently and asserting MDC inside the stage; log Thread.currentThread().getName() with MDC; a debugger watch on the static field.
  5. Root cause: Three independent defects. (1) The snapshot is static, so every request would reuse the first request's context; the wrong-user rate of 0.3% means it surfaces when stages run inline on threads that already hold other contexts. (2) MDC is mutated on the caller thread and never restored, polluting request threads in Tomcat's pool for later requests. (3) Nothing propagates SecurityContext, which is also thread-local; and the trace ID isn't in MDC on the worker so logs lack it.
  6. Fix: Short-term: capture per submission, set inside the runnable, restore in finally:
Executor ctxExec = r -> {
    Map<String,String> ctx = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
    SecurityContext sc = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
    pool.execute(() -> {
        Map<String,String> prev = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
        SecurityContext prevSc = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
        try {
            if (ctx != null) MDC.setContextMap(ctx); else MDC.clear();
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(sc);
            r.run();
        } finally {
            if (prev != null) MDC.setContextMap(prev); else MDC.clear();
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(prevSc);
        }
    });
};

Long-term: use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService and Micrometer context-propagation (or OpenTelemetry's Context.taskWrapping) for MDC and span context. 7. Prevention: A test fixture that runs two concurrent requests with different MDC and asserts isolation; a ban on static mutable context; a lint/review rule "all executors for request work must come from ExecutorFactory". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set SecurityContextHolder strategy to MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL: it copies on thread creation only, so pooled threads would reuse the first caller's identity. I would not clean up logs retroactively without also notifying whoever consumes audit data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Stage runs thenApply inline on a different pool's thread? → It sees that thread's context; make stages that need context Async with the wrapping executor, or avoid reading thread-locals in stages by passing values explicitly.
  • Virtual threads? → Thread-locals work but are per virtual thread; context must still be copied when you start a new task; structured concurrency inherits scoped values.
  • Cost? → Copying a small MDC map per task is microseconds; irrelevant against a 50 ms remote call.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An audit trail showed a support agent's ID against customer actions. The root cause was a thread-local never cleared on pooled workers; the lesson was that a context leak is a security bug, not a logging nuisance.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Passes IDs as method args, misses the data leak.
  • Hire: Identifies static snapshot and wrong-thread set; fixes with capture-and-restore.
  • Strong hire: Calls it a security incident, handles security and span contexts, and explains why inheritable thread locals fail with pools.

questions.contextHtml: Product asks: "The home page should show recommendations, promotions and loyalty points. It must load in under 300 ms. Show whatever we have." Current backends: recommendations p50 90 ms / p99 700 ms, promotions p50 40 ms / p99 150 ms, loyalty points p50 60 ms / p99 400 ms. Traffic 1,200 RPS. The first implementation uses allOf with no timeouts and the page p99 is 780 ms. Loyalty points must be accurate if shown (money-related); recommendations are optional.
questions.promptHtml: How do you design the aggregation to meet the 300 ms goal, and what clarifications do you need from the product team?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add orTimeout(300ms) to everything and return nulls." That ignores per-component requirements and the cost of abandoned work.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 300 ms for p50, p99 or a hard deadline? What does "whatever we have" mean for loyalty points: omit, or show stale? Can we serve cached/stale recommendations? What is the acceptable degraded-response rate (e.g. under 2%)? Does the downstream team tolerate 3x request fan-out?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start the three calls in parallel today and set a global deadline; this alone moves latency from the sum to the max.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The p99 780 ms is dominated by recommendations' tail (700 ms) plus overhead; promotions are never the problem; loyalty tail 400 ms alone exceeds the budget.
  4. How I'd verify each: Existing traces for the worst requests; per-dependency latency histograms in Micrometer; run a k6 test at 1,200 RPS against a staging stack with injected latency.
  5. Root cause: Waiting for the slowest component with no deadline; page latency equals the slowest dependency's tail.
  6. Fix: Per-component budgets under one deadline. Required component (loyalty): stale-while-revalidate from cache with a 250 ms timeout, fall back to the last known value marked "as of". Optional components: completeOnTimeout with empty/cached results at 200 ms.
long deadlineNanos = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(300);
var recs  = recsClient.fetch(uid, io).completeOnTimeout(Recs.EMPTY, 200, MILLISECONDS);
var promo = promoClient.fetch(uid, io).completeOnTimeout(Promo.NONE, 150, MILLISECONDS);
var pts   = loyalty.fetch(uid, io).orTimeout(250, MILLISECONDS)
                   .exceptionally(e -> cache.lastKnownPoints(uid));
HomePage page = recs.thenCombine(promo, Pair::of)
    .thenCombine(pts, (rp, p) -> new HomePage(rp.a(), rp.b(), p))
    .join();   // at the edge only

Each client must also have its own read timeout so abandoned calls free their threads. Return the response with a flag listing which sections degraded, and emit a metric per section. 7. Prevention: SLO on degraded-section rate, an alert when recommendations fall back more than 5%, load tests with latency injection, circuit breakers per dependency. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not fail the whole page when an optional section times out, and I would not show potentially wrong loyalty points; stale-but-labelled is a product decision I'd confirm. Hedged requests (sending a duplicate after p95) could cut the recommendations tail but add load; I'd propose it only after caching.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Recommendations p99 gets worse, 10x traffic? → Circuit breaker opens, serve cached/popular items; the 200 ms timeout alone would keep leaked work running, so the breaker protects the pool.
  • Why completeOnTimeout over orTimeout + exceptionally? → Same effect for defaults; orTimeout when I want to log/count the timeout as an error.
  • Deadline vs per-call timeouts? → The sum of per-call budgets can exceed the page deadline when stages are sequential; carry a remaining-time budget.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dashboard met its SLO in tests but not in production because the slowest widget was optional; once the team labelled widgets required/optional and gave each a budget, p99 dropped from 900 ms to 280 ms without touching the backends.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One timeout on everything, null for failures.
  • Hire: Parallel calls, per-component timeouts and fallbacks, distinguishes required from optional.
  • Strong hire: Asks the right product questions, budgets under a deadline, handles abandoned work and amplification, adds metrics and an SLO for degradation.

questions.promptHtml: For a long chain of CompletableFuture stages, precisely how does the runtime decide which thread runs each stage, and what surprises does that produce (ordering, stack depth, running on the wrong thread)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who have read the implementation model from those who memorized the API. L3 candidates predict behaviour rather than test it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each future keeps a lock-free stack of dependent completions. When a future completes, the completing thread pops and runs them inline, which is why non-async stages run on whichever thread finished the source. If I attach a stage to an already-completed future, it runs immediately on my thread. Multiple dependents of one future run in LIFO order, so I must not depend on ordering, and a stage that completes another future can run that future's dependents inline too."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Implementation model (OpenJDK, java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; internals can change, so treat as behaviour description not API contract):

  • Each stage is a Completion object pushed onto the source's stack with CAS (lock-free Treiber stack).
  • postComplete() drains the stack. For a dependent whose own dependents are pending, it moves them onto the current drain loop rather than recursing, to avoid stack overflow on long chains. Because the stack is LIFO, dependents attached later typically run first.
  • *Async variants push a task to the executor instead of executing inline.
  • complete() is itself the point where inline execution happens: calling cf.complete(v) from your IO thread runs all non-async dependents on that thread before complete returns.

Surprises:

  1. Inline cost on your thread: cf.complete(v) in a Netty handler runs user stages in the handler thread. A blocking stage stalls the event loop.
  2. No ordering guarantee: f.thenAccept(a); f.thenAccept(b); may run b before a.
  3. Reentrancy: A stage that calls other.complete(...) runs other's dependents on this thread, nested in the first stage's execution. A mistake in one stage can spill into unrelated code.
  4. Timeouts: orTimeout completion runs dependents on the single timer thread unless the stages are async, so heavy fallbacks should be Async.
  5. Already-completed fast path: Unit tests with completedFuture run everything on the test thread and hide threading bugs that production has.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CompletableFuture<String> src = new CompletableFuture<>();
src.thenAccept(s -> System.out.println("A " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));
src.thenAccept(s -> System.out.println("B " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));
// Output order after complete() is not specified; commonly B before A on current JDKs.
src.complete("x");

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Depending on dependent ordering.
  • Heavy stages after orTimeout, running on the timer thread.
  • Testing with completed futures only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you force stages onto a dedicated pool? → Use *Async(fn, executor) everywhere, or a subclass overriding defaultExecutor().
  2. What does newIncompleteFuture() do for subclasses? → Lets a subclass make derived stages of its own type so overrides apply across the chain.
  3. How would you make timing deterministic in tests? → Use controllable executors and incomplete futures completed by the test.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "thenApply runs on the same thread". Senior can say whose thread, in what order, and what happens on nested completion, and designs around it (async hops for anything non-trivial).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A completion callback in an HTTP client thread ran a database call inline via a non-async stage; the whole client stalled under load while the CPU stayed idle.

questions.promptHtml: What does cancel() on a CompletableFuture really do? How do you build cancellation that actually stops work, including through a chain?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The assumption "cancel stops it" is wrong for CompletableFuture and causes leaked work during timeouts and client disconnects.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "cancel just completes that future with CancellationException; the mayInterruptIfRunning flag is ignored by the documented contract because the future does not control the thread running the computation. The upstream task keeps running, and cancelling a downstream stage does not cancel its source. To really stop work I hold the underlying handle (a Future from the executor, an HTTP call object), make the task interruptible or check a flag, and wire cancellation myself."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the Java 21 Javadoc: cancel(boolean) is equivalent to completeExceptionally(new CancellationException()), and mayInterruptIfRunning has no effect. After cancel, isCancelled(), isDone() and isCompletedExceptionally() are all true.

Direction of propagation:

 src --thenApply--> mid --thenApply--> dst
 dst.cancel()  : only dst is cancelled. src and mid keep running; their results are discarded.
 src.cancel()  : src fails; mid and dst complete exceptionally with CompletionException(CancellationException).

So cancellation flows downstream (as a failure), not upstream. Also supplyAsync returns a future that is not the FutureTask in the executor, so there is nothing to interrupt.

Making it real:

  1. Submit to the executor yourself to get a Future (or FutureTask) with interrupt support, then link: when the CF completes exceptionally, cancel the Future with true.
  2. Make the task cooperate: check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() or use interruptible blocking calls; an HTTP client call must be given a cancel handle.
  3. In chains, for each stage that owns work, keep the handle. A "cancel scope" object that holds all handles is the usual pattern. Structured concurrency (JEP 453, a preview API in 21 and later, verify status in your release) provides this natively: when a scope shuts down, unfinished subtasks are interrupted.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static <T> CompletableFuture<T> cancellable(Callable<T> task, ExecutorService ex) {
    CompletableFuture<T> cf = new CompletableFuture<>();
    Future<?> handle = ex.submit(() -> {
        try { cf.complete(task.call()); }
        catch (Throwable t) { cf.completeExceptionally(t); }
    });
    cf.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (cf.isCancelled()) handle.cancel(true); });
    return cf;
}
// Timeout path: .orTimeout() completes exceptionally with TimeoutException, not a cancellation,
// so check cf.isCompletedExceptionally() if you also want to interrupt on timeout.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling cancel(true) and assuming CPU is freed.
  • Cancelling a downstream stage and expecting the HTTP request upstream to abort.
  • Forgetting that orTimeout produces TimeoutException, not cancellation, so a isCancelled() check does not fire.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to the result of a task whose future was cancelled? → It runs to completion; complete returns false and the value is discarded.
  2. How do you cancel work on client disconnect in Servlet async? → Register an AsyncListener.onError/onComplete, and trigger your cancel scope.
  3. How do reactive types compare? → Reactor/RxJava subscriptions carry cancellation upstream by design; CF does not.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "cancel(true) interrupts". Senior knows the flag is ignored, which direction propagation goes, and builds handle-based cancellation or uses structured concurrency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Abandoned requests kept doing 8-second database queries after clients timed out at 1 second, because "cancelled" futures only cancelled the waiting.

questions.promptHtml: Compare thread-per-request with blocking calls, CompletableFuture composition, reactive streams and virtual threads for a service that fans out to several downstream services. How do you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks architectural judgment, not API recall. Strong candidates name costs (debuggability, backpressure, pinning) and do not pick a fashion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Thread-per-request with blocking calls is simplest but limited by platform thread count. CompletableFuture gives parallel fan-out inside a request but still blocks threads on IO unless the client is truly non-blocking. Reactive gives end-to-end non-blocking with backpressure and few threads, at a big cost in code complexity and debuggability. Virtual threads, final in Java 21, bring back simple blocking code with cheap threads. For a new Java 21+ service I default to virtual threads for IO-bound request handling and use CompletableFuture or structured concurrency only for explicit parallel fan-out."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Model Threads blocked on IO? Code style Backpressure Debugging Best for
Blocking, platform threads yes (1 thread per in-flight request) sequential implicit via pool limit easy stack traces modest concurrency (hundreds)
CompletableFuture + blocking client yes, but parallel callback chains manual stack traces lose causality fan-out inside request
CompletableFuture + non-blocking client no callback chains manual hard libraries that already return CF
Reactive (Reactor/RxJava, WebFlux) no operator pipelines built in hardest streaming, high connection counts, backpressure needs
Virtual threads (Java 21) the virtual thread parks, the carrier is freed sequential none built-in; bound with Semaphore normal stack traces and thread dumps (JSON dump via jcmd Thread.dump_to_file) IO-bound request handling at 10k+ concurrency

Little's law frames it: concurrency = throughput x latency. At 2,000 RPS with 200 ms of downstream latency you need 400 concurrent requests in flight. 400 platform threads is fine (about 1 MB reserved stack each by default on 64-bit Linux, verify via -Xss); at 20,000 RPS you need 4,000, where memory and scheduling overhead start to hurt. Virtual threads make 4,000 or 40,000 cheap, while CPU-bound work still needs cores.

Caveats for virtual threads: pinning when blocked inside synchronized (fixed by JEP 491 in JDK 24 per OpenJDK; on 21 use ReentrantLock or check with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads), unbounded concurrency overwhelms downstream, thread-locals still work but are per virtual thread, and CPU-bound code gains nothing. CompletableFuture still has a role as a composition and result container: you can run stages on Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Details in the Virtual Threads chunk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Java 21: simple blocking code, CF only for explicit fan-out
try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    var a = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> svcA.call(), vt);
    var b = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> svcB.call(), vt);
    return a.thenCombine(b, Merged::new).join();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing blocking calls into a reactive pipeline on the event loop.
  • Choosing reactive for "performance" on a service that is not connection-bound.
  • Putting virtual threads in front of a connection pool of 20 and calling it scalable; the pool is the limit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is reactive still the better choice? → Streaming with backpressure, very high fan-in of long-lived connections, or an existing reactive ecosystem.
  2. Do virtual threads make CompletableFuture obsolete? → No. They remove the need for async to save threads, not the need to express parallel composition and timeouts.
  3. What bounds concurrency with virtual threads? → Explicit limits: Semaphore, bounded connection pools, rate limiters, bulkheads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "reactive is non-blocking so it's faster". Senior frames by concurrency math, team cost, debuggability and downstream limits, and says that the bottleneck usually moves to the database or the connection pool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team rewrote a service to WebFlux for throughput; a single blocking JDBC call on the event loop caused 5 s stalls, which they eventually fixed by moving to a Java 21 virtual-thread executor with simpler code.

questions.contextHtml:
An order-enrichment service (4 vCPU pods, 12 pods, ~900 RPS) calls inventory, pricing and shipping via CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.get(...)) with no executor. At 14:05 pricing began taking 8 to 12 s per call (normally 60 ms). Within 90 seconds, /enrich p99 went from 250 ms to 30 s, health checks to /health still return in 5 ms, and CPU is at 6%. A nightly report job in the same JVM using parallelStream() also hangs. A thread dump shows:

"ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1" #31 daemon  WAITING/RUNNABLE
   at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0(Native Method)
   at ... pricing client
"ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-2" ... (same)
"ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3" ... (same)
"http-nio-8080-exec-17" WAITING at CompletableFuture$Signaller.block

Only 3 commonPool-worker threads exist.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose the incident, stop the bleeding and prevent recurrence.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the pods and add more pods." Restart buys minutes; the failure repeats when pricing is slow again, and more pods amplify load on pricing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it all 12 pods? (Same code, so likely yes.) Any deploy at 14:00? What do inventory and shipping latencies look like? What timeouts does the HTTP client have? Which other features use the common pool?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn off the pricing step via flag or return cached prices; restart is a fallback. Rolling back is useless if code was unchanged; the trigger was the dependency, not our deploy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Common pool starved: 3 workers (4 vCPU - 1) all stuck in pricing sockets; (b) HTTP client has no/long read timeout; (c) request threads blocked on join() waiting for starved stages; (d) pricing outage itself (true, but the blast radius is our design).
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.print x3, 10 s apart, counting commonPool-worker states; ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getQueuedSubmissionCount() via JMX/actuator; check parallelism with ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism() (expect 3); client config for read timeout; Micrometer metrics for inventory/shipping call rates, which fall to zero.
  5. Root cause: All async stages share a JVM-wide pool of 3 threads. Pricing calls of ~10 s each holding a thread mean the pool does 0.3 calls/s in total, while 900 RPS x 12 pods is needed, so every stage (including inventory and shipping) queues behind pricing: one slow dependency took down all three. Request threads then block on join() and the Tomcat pool fills. CPU is idle because everything waits on sockets.
  6. Fix: Short-term: set client read timeout to 500 ms and orTimeout; circuit breaker around pricing with a cache fallback. Medium-term: dedicated bounded executors per dependency (bulkhead):
ExecutorService pricingEx = bounded("pricing", 40, 80); // threads, queue
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(sku), pricingEx)
    .orTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .exceptionally(e -> pricingCache.get(sku));

Sizing for pricing: 900 RPS / 12 pods = 75 RPS per pod x 0.06 s = 4.5 busy threads at normal latency; 40 threads gives roughly 9x headroom without letting one dependency consume every thread. 7. Prevention: Ban default-executor async calls via an ArchUnit rule or a wrapper; pool metrics (active/queue/rejected) alerts; chaos test with pricing latency injected to 10 s; timeout budget reviews in design review. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism to 200; that hides the missing timeout and bulkhead and still shares fate with parallel streams. I would not retry on timeout without backoff and a retry budget, as that multiplies load on pricing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pods are 1 vCPU? → Parallelism below two means a new thread per task (per the Javadoc), so no starvation but unbounded threads under load and likely OOM or native thread limits.
  • Only pricing is slow, but inventory fails too: why? → Shared pool; the bulkhead makes failures independent.
  • Can virtual threads fix this? → They remove the thread cap but then a slow pricing call would hold 10 s of in-flight work per request unbounded; still need timeouts and a semaphore.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's "async" refactor looked fine in staging with a 4 ms stub. In production a single dependency's brownout silently turned a 3-thread pool into a global lock. After the incident every outbound client got its own named pool, a timeout and a breaker, in that order.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Restart and scale out only.
  • Hire: Identifies common pool starvation, adds timeouts and a dedicated executor.
  • Strong hire: Computes pool capacity vs demand, designs bulkheads and breaker fallbacks, notes the parallelism edge cases, and builds prevention checks.

questions.contextHtml: A recommendation gateway handles 500 RPS, calling a ranking service with orTimeout(200ms) and one retry on timeout. Ranking's p50 is 40 ms and p99 150 ms; it runs at 55% CPU on 8 pods. The gateway's executor is 64 threads with a queue of 1,000, client read timeout is the library default (30 s). Marketing plans a campaign that will take traffic to 5,000 RPS (10x). In a load test at 3,000 RPS, ranking's p99 hits 900 ms, the gateway reports ~60% timeouts, ranking CPU is 100%, and the gateway executor shows 64 active, queue 1,000, rejections climbing.
questions.promptHtml: Why does a 6x load increase produce a collapse rather than a degradation, and what do you change before the campaign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale ranking 10x." That ignores the retry amplification and abandoned work, so it may still collapse and it costs far more than needed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the campaign traffic cache-friendly (same items)? Can we serve a degraded generic list? What is ranking's headroom? Are retries idempotent-safe? What is the business cost of a degraded response vs an error?
  2. Immediate mitigation (for the load test or an incident): Disable the retry, lower client read timeout to match 200 ms, and enable the cached/popular fallback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Retry on timeout doubles load when ranking slows, creating a positive feedback loop; (b) orTimeout abandons the future but not the HTTP call (30 s read timeout), so abandoned requests still consume ranking capacity and gateway threads; (c) queue of 1,000 adds seconds of waiting before work begins, so most tasks time out before they even start; (d) ranking itself saturates at some RPS.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare gateway outgoing request rate vs incoming RPS (expect ~2x at the failure point); thread dump of the gateway pool showing threads in socket reads far beyond 200 ms; executor queue wait metric; ranking's CPU and queue; k6 ramps with and without retry.
  5. Root cause: A metastable overload. Math: at 3,000 RPS with the retry on timeout, offered load to ranking rises toward 3,000 x (1 + p_timeout); with p_timeout 0.6 that is about 4,800 RPS, beyond ranking's capacity (roughly 8 pods at 55% CPU handling 500 RPS suggests a limit near 900 RPS, so that is just under 1,000 RPS sustained: verify with a saturation test). Latency rises, more timeouts, more retries. The gateway's 64 threads x 30 s read timeout means each stuck call pins a thread for far longer than the 200 ms deadline: with 64 threads, capacity drops to 64 / 30 s ≈ 2 calls/s if all calls hang. The 1,000-deep queue at even 100 calls/s completes in 10 s, far beyond the 200 ms deadline: serving requests already doomed.
  6. Fix: (1) Client timeouts equal to the deadline (connect 50 ms, read 200 ms) so threads free when callers give up. (2) Retry budget (retries at most 10% of requests) with jittered backoff, only for idempotent calls and only when the first attempt failed fast. (3) Short bounded queue (for example 32) with AbortPolicy and drop-on-dequeue if the deadline passed. (4) Load shedding / circuit breaker with a cached popular-items fallback. (5) Capacity: autoscale ranking to the real throughput needed, e.g. 5,000 RPS cache-miss traffic only, after caching, maybe 1,500 RPS.
  7. Prevention: Load tests at 2x expected peak with injected latency; alert on retry ratio; SLO-based autoscaling; game-day before the campaign.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not simply increase the pool and queue: more concurrency into a saturated service lengthens everyone's latency. I would not retry on timeouts at all for a saturated downstream; a degraded answer is better than doubling load.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ranking is a shared service owned by another team? → Negotiate a quota, apply client-side rate limiting and a bulkhead so we cannot take it down.
  • Hedged requests to cut tail latency? → Only with a budget (e.g. send a second request after p95 for 5% of calls); they add load, which is dangerous during saturation.
  • Can virtual threads help? → They remove the thread cap but the abandoned-work and retry-amplification mechanisms are unchanged; we would need a Semaphore limit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A campaign launch passed every test at steady load and failed in the first minute: the retry that "improved reliability" at 1x multiplied traffic at the first slowdown. The post-mortem action was a company-wide retry budget standard.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scale the service, increase pool.
  • Hire: Spots retry amplification and read-timeout mismatch; shortens queue; adds fallback.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies amplification, explains metastable failure and deadline-aware queues, proposes retry budgets and testing at 2x with fault injection.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem draft: "Between 02:10 and 09:40 about 11,000 orders were charged but never got a confirmation email or an inventory decrement. No alerts fired, error rate stayed at 0.02%, and the order API returned 200." The relevant code:

public OrderResponse place(Order o) {
    Payment p = payments.charge(o);
    CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> inventory.decrement(o))
        .thenRun(() -> emailService.sendConfirmation(o));   // returned future dropped
    return OrderResponse.ok(p.id());
}

A dependency upgrade at 02:05 changed inventory.decrement to throw IllegalStateException("schema v3 required"). The app runs runAsync on the common pool.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: how did this go unnoticed, what are the contributing factors, and what changes do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a try/catch." That fixes one line but not the design of fire-and-forget work, delivery guarantees or observability.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What delivery guarantee does the business need for inventory and email? Is the work idempotent? Can the payment and inventory be one transaction? Do we have an outbox or queue? What alerts exist on business metrics (orders vs emails)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the dependency; identify affected orders from payment records minus inventory events; run a repair job that is idempotent (decrement keyed by order ID) and send delayed confirmations; notify support.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Exception in runAsync stored in the future, never observed; (b) thenRun skipped because the source failed, so no email either; (c) no business-level monitor; (d) the upgrade lacked integration tests for that call.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce locally: runAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException(); }) produces a failed future that nothing logs; check logs for the exception (absent); count payments vs inventory events vs email sends per hour.
  5. Root cause: A failed CompletableFuture whose result nobody reads is silent. Unlike a Thread with an uncaught exception handler, the exception is captured into the future. The code also treated "charged" as complete while the follow-up work had no guarantee at all (lost if the JVM restarts, too).
  6. Fix: Short-term: terminal handler on every chain.
CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> inventory.decrement(o), ex)
    .thenRunAsync(() -> email.sendConfirmation(o), ex)
    .whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (e != null) { log.error("post-order failed {}", o.id(), e);
                                               metrics.counter("order.postwork.failed").increment(); } });

Long-term: do not rely on in-memory async for obligations. Write an outbox row in the same DB transaction as the order; a relay publishes to a queue; consumers are idempotent with retries and a dead-letter queue. Use in-process async only for best-effort work. 7. Prevention: Static check: find ignored CompletableFuture return values (Error Prone FutureReturnValueIgnored); business-invariant alerts (orders without inventory event after 5 minutes); contract tests for dependency upgrades; a canary with synthetic orders. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the API call wait for inventory and email (adds latency and couples availability). I would not "fix" it only by logging: logs without alerts are only evidence after the fact. An outbox adds operational complexity (relay, ordering, duplicates) and I'd accept that for money-adjacent flows.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the 0.02% error rate not move? → The exception never reached the request thread; error rate measures HTTP responses, not background work.
  • Is exceptionally(log) enough? → It handles the logging but not retries or durability; process crash still loses the work.
  • What about @Async in Spring? → Same issue for void methods unless an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler is set; for methods returning a Future, the caller must observe it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reconciliation job found a gap between payments and shipments that had existed for months; in-memory "fire and forget" had lost the work at every deploy. An outbox plus a per-hour invariant check ended the class of bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds a try/catch.
  • Hire: Explains the silent failed future, adds terminal handling and alerting.
  • Strong hire: Separates best-effort from must-happen work, proposes outbox with idempotency, invariant-based monitoring, repair plan and lint rules.

questions.contextHtml: A pricing API (Java 17, Spring Boot, Tomcat, 16 vCPU / 8 GB pods, 24 pods, 6,000 RPS) uses CompletableFuture chains over a 200-thread io executor for 5 downstream calls per request, p99 180 ms. The team wants to move to Java 21 virtual threads to simplify code and cut the pod count. Known facts: some libraries use synchronized around JDBC/HTTP calls (a legacy rate limiter and a vendor SDK), the DB pool (HikariCP) is 50 connections per pod, and the code relies on ThreadLocal for MDC. A canary on Java 21 with virtual threads shows p99 spikes to 2 s every few minutes while CPU stays low.
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan the migration and explain the canary spikes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Virtual threads are lightweight, just enable them." That ignores pinning, downstream limits and the 50-connection DB pool, and does not use the canary evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which JDK exactly (21 vs 24+, since JEP 491 changes synchronized pinning)? Which libraries use synchronized or native calls around blocking IO? What do downstreams tolerate in concurrency? Is there a stop condition on the canary?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pull the canary back to the platform thread executor (a config flag), keeping the Java 21 runtime; the spike is in the concurrency model, not the JDK.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Pinning: a virtual thread blocked inside synchronized pins its carrier; with carriers by default equal to cores (16), 16 pinned threads freeze all virtual threads; (b) DB pool contention: thousands of virtual threads now queue on 50 connections; (c) downstream overload because concurrency is no longer capped at 200; (d) GC or memory effects from more in-flight requests.
  4. How I'd verify each: JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned and -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full on Java 21; jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json; Hikari metrics (pending threads, connection acquire time); downstream concurrency graphs; carrier saturation via jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism and maxPoolSize settings (system properties of the default scheduler, verify defaults for your release).
  5. Root cause (most likely): The vendor SDK's synchronized block around a socket read pins carriers. Spikes every few minutes match the SDK's periodic token refresh holding the monitor for ~1.5 s. While pinned, the default scheduler may compensate for some blocking but not for pinned monitor waits, so with 16 carriers busy all virtual threads stall; CPU stays low as everything waits on IO.
  6. Fix: Short-term: wrap/replace the legacy limiter with ReentrantLock; isolate the vendor SDK on a small dedicated platform-thread executor and call it through a bounded bridge; add a Semaphore limiting in-flight requests (for example 300 per pod) and per-dependency semaphores. Long-term: move to Java 24+ where synchronized no longer pins in most cases (JEP 491; verify the exact scope), then re-test.
// Bound downstream concurrency explicitly; virtual threads do not do this for you
private final Semaphore pricingPermits = new Semaphore(120);
Price call(String sku) throws InterruptedException {
    if (!pricingPermits.tryAcquire(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new OverloadedException();
    try { return pricingClient.get(sku); } finally { pricingPermits.release(); }
}

Plan: feature flag per executor, canary 1 pod then 5%, compare p99, error rate, DB wait, GC; roll forward only when VirtualThreadPinned events stay under an agreed rate. Keep CompletableFuture for fan-out (run stages on newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()), or switch to structured concurrency only once its API is final in your release (preview in 21; verify). 7. Prevention: JFR in CI load tests asserting zero long pins; dependency review for synchronized+IO; metrics on semaphore waits; propagate MDC explicitly since each virtual thread has its own thread-locals. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove the 50-connection DB bound to "use" virtual threads; Hikari protects the database. I would not promise a pod-count reduction up front: pods are CPU-bound after the IO wait is removed, and savings must be measured. I would not migrate all pools at once.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can we pool virtual threads? → No; they are cheap. Pooling them defeats the model; bound concurrency with semaphores instead.
  • Thread-locals with 100k virtual threads? → Memory scales with the number of threads times the thread-local size; prefer passing data explicitly or scoped values where available.
  • CPU-bound endpoints? → Virtual threads add nothing; keep a platform pool of about cores for them.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A canary looked healthy on average and failed on the tail every ten minutes: one vendor library's token refresh held a monitor for two seconds. JFR's pinned-thread event named the stack in one capture, and the fix was a three-line ReentrantLock swap in a fork.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Just flip the flag", ignores canary evidence.
  • Hire: Identifies pinning with a verification method and bounds concurrency with semaphores.
  • Strong hire: Explains carriers and parallelism, DB and downstream limits, staged rollout with stop conditions, JDK-version-dependent behaviour, and honest savings expectations.
